newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Anti-government Albanians keep up pressure.
newsitem.headline: Anti-government Albanians keep up pressure.

text.p: Sporadic violence, a blockade of Albania's main north-south road and anti-government protests in numerous southern towns kept tensions high on Friday in the crisis-hit Balkan country.

A teenager was stabbed during a 10th day of protests in the seaside town of Vlore, 150 km (85 miles) south of Tirana. Three people were killed and 150 were injured during clashes with riot police in Vlore earlier this week.
Witnesses said Adnan Gjoni, 17, was stabbed in the neck and shoulder after accusing a man in the crowd of being a secret policeman. He was in hospital but out of danger.

Vlore mayor Gezim Zile, a member of the ruling Democratic Party, called for the government to resign over its failure to contain a month-long crisis over the collapse of dubious investment schemes which left many Albanians destitute.

"They have done nothing to help the people. They must go," Zile told Reuters. He was the first mayor from the ruling party to call for the government of Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi to quit and for a new cabinet to be formed.
Scuffles broke out in Fier, also south of Tirana, when 100 riot police tried to keep several thousand protesters from the town's square.
Protesters, enraged after men attacked a demonstration on Thursday, threw stones at police trying to keep them from the square. Police quickly gave ground, leaving an uneasy calm.
About 5,000 people demonstrated in Fier and 7,000 in Vlore. Both groups chanted: "Down with (President Sali) Berisha", "We want our money back" and "Thieves, thieves."
Demonstrators erected three barricades on the north-south road between Fier and Vlore, cutting the main link between the country's second port and the capital in Tirana.

Anti-government demonstrations were reported in several other towns around the country. Several hundred protesters in the southern town of Gjirokaster lit candles in the evening and formed the word "Vlore" in a show of solidarity.
Hundreds of people bouquets of flowers turned out in Elbasan, south of Tirana. One of the slogans of the main opposition Forum for Democracy is "With flowers not stones."
Albania, Europe's poorest country, has been swept for the past month by protests and riots by investors who lost their life savings in failed high-risk pyramid investment schemes.
The schemes lured new money with offers of high interest rates and then used the cash to pay earlier investors. A large proportion of Albania's adults seem to have put their money into the funds.
Investors now blame Berisha's party for letting the schemes flourish and opposition parties accuse him of using cash from the schemes to finance his election campaign last year.

The government, in turn, says opposition groups are trying to exploit the crisis. It impounded about $300 million from two failed funds but has steadfastly refused to use government money to reimburse luckless investors.

The head of the state Savings Bank, Dedri Collaku, said $4.3 million had been distributed so far to investors in the failed Populli scheme. The government froze more than $100 million of Populli's assets last month.

The Forum for Democracy oppositon snubbed Deputy Prime Minister Tritan Shehu by refusing to attend all-party talks to discuss the crisis. Five smaller right-wing parties did take part and demanded the resignation of Meksi's government.
Meksi seems determined to weather the crisis but diplomats said the scale of the financial collapse could be enormous and the government might find controlling popular unrest difficult.
Shehu again blamed the protests on the Forum opposition, accusing them of "terrorist acts and political manipulation of the people and politically exploiting a fabricated situation."
Some estimates put the losses from the collapsed schemes at $2 billion, about the size of Albania's annual gross domestic product.
